Goedert for 13 yards; on the next snap, without a huddle, he hit DeVonta Smith for 23. FTN charted both throws
as RPOs. It also charted them as play-action, and it charted Hurts's 45-yard touchdown to A.J. Brown early in
the second quarter as an RPO too, a reminder of how blurry the line between the two families is in
charting.[^sb57]

**What to notice:** how Hurts's legs change the read. With a quarterback who can also keep on a zone read, the
backside end and the overhang defender both have to respect him, so a single snap can carry a give, a keep and
a throw.
:::

## What the numbers say

The NFL's play-by-play doesn't say whether a play was an RPO: a handoff is a handoff and a pass is a pass. But
FTN's charters, who watch every NFL play, flag RPOs, and the flag is in the nflverse data from 2022 on. The
numbers come with a caveat that is worth learning once: **charting services disagree.** PFF's rates for the
same seasons run well above FTN's (about 8 to 10.5 percent of plays against FTN's 4 to 6), because deciding from film whether a handoff "was" an RPO (did a receiver
run a real route? was the quarterback reading someone?) is a judgment, and charters judge differently. Use
one series at a time, and compare teams within it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rpo-data
#| fig-cap: "RPOs in FTN's NFL charting. Left: the share of each team's offensive plays charted as RPOs, 2025 regular season (runs and passes, scrambles included, kneel-downs and spikes excluded). Right: how far past the line RPO throws travel in the air, against all other passes, 2022–2025 regular seasons; air yards at or behind zero (shaded) are thrown to a receiver at or behind the line of scrimmage. RPO throws pile up behind the line, the bubbles and now screens that NFL timing favors; other passes spread far downfield. (The bump at the right edge of the 'all other passes' line is the last bin, which holds every throw of 30 or more air yards.) Data: nflverse play-by-play joined to FTN charting (load_ftn_charting) via nflreadpy; FTN's RPO flag is a charter's judgment, and other services count more RPOs."
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

style.apply()
SEASONS = [2022, 2023, 2024, 2025]
ftn = nfl().load_ftn_charting(SEASONS).to_pandas().rename(
    columns={"nflverse_game_id": "game_id", "nflverse_play_id": "play_id"})
ftn["is_rpo"] = ftn["is_rpo"].fillna(False).astype(bool)
cols = ["season", "season_type", "game_id", "play_id", "posteam", "play_type", "epa", "success", "air_yards",
        "down", "penalty_type", "complete_pass", "shotgun"]
allp = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
allp = allp[allp["season_type"] == "REG"]
reg = allp[allp["play_type"].isin(["pass", "run"]) & allp["down"].notna()]
m = reg.merge(ftn[["game_id", "play_id", "is_rpo", "n_defense_box", "is_screen_pass"]],
              on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
rpo = m[m["is_rpo"]]
rate = m.groupby("season")["is_rpo"].mean()
team25 = m[m["season"] == 2025].groupby("posteam")["is_rpo"].mean().sort_values()
lead = {s: m[m["season"] == s].groupby("posteam")["is_rpo"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False)
        for s in SEASONS}
thrown = rpo[(rpo["play_type"] == "pass") & rpo["air_yards"].notna()]
other = m[(~m["is_rpo"]) & (m["play_type"] == "pass") & m["air_yards"].notna()]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.9), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.0, 1.25]))
ax = axes[0]
hi = {"KC"}
ax.barh(range(len(team25)), team25.values * 100,
        color=[style.SERIES[0] if t in hi else "#9ec5f4" for t in team25.index], height=0.72)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(team25)))
ax.set_yticklabels(team25.index, fontsize=6.2)
ax.axvline(rate[2025] * 100, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)))
ax.text(rate[2025] * 100 + 0.3, 1.0, f"league\n{rate[2025]:.1%}", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2, va="center")
ax.set_xlabel("% of plays charted as RPO, 2025", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("RPO rate by team, 2025", fontsize=9.5)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, len(team25) - 0.3)
ax = axes[1]
bins = np.arange(-8, 31)
for d_, name, col in [(thrown, "RPO throws", style.SERIES[0]), (other, "All other passes", style.SERIES[1])]:
    a = d_["air_yards"].clip(-8, 30)
    share = a.round().value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(bins, fill_value=0) * 100
    ax.step(bins, share.values, where="mid", color=col, lw=1.8, label=name)
ax.axvspan(-8.5, 0.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.6, zorder=0)
ax.text(-4.0, 15.6, "at or behind\nthe line", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-8.5, 30.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 17.5)
ax.set_xlabel("air yards (30 = 30 or more)", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_ylabel("% of throws", fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_title("How far RPO throws go, 2022–2025", fontsize=9.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=7.2, loc="upper right")
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.4)
plt.show()

behind_r, behind_o = (thrown["air_yards"] <= 0).mean(), (other["air_yards"] <= 0).mean()
deep_r, deep_o = (thrown["air_yards"] > 10).mean(), (other["air_yards"] > 10).mean()
gave25 = (rpo.loc[rpo["season"] == 2025, "play_type"] == "run").mean()
gave_all = (rpo["play_type"] == "run").mean()
epa_pass, epa_run = rpo.loc[rpo["play_type"] == "pass", "epa"].mean(), rpo.loc[rpo["play_type"] == "run", "epa"].mean()
comp_r = thrown["complete_pass"].mean()
epa_rpo, epa_non = rpo["epa"].mean(), m.loc[~m["is_rpo"], "epa"].mean()
sr_rpo, sr_non = rpo["success"].mean(), m.loc[~m["is_rpo"], "success"].mean()
idp = allp[allp["penalty_type"].fillna("").eq("Ineligible Downfield Pass")]
idp = idp.merge(ftn[["game_id", "play_id", "is_rpo"]], on=["game_id", "play_id"], how="inner")
idp_n, idp_rpo = len(idp), idp["is_rpo"].mean()
rpo_share = m["is_rpo"].mean()
box_thrown = {k: (rpo.loc[rpo["n_defense_box"] == k, "play_type"] == "pass").mean() for k in (6, 7)}
box_thrown[8] = (rpo.loc[rpo["n_defense_box"] >= 8, "play_type"] == "pass").mean()
kc25, phi22, ind23 = lead[2025].get("KC"), lead[2022].get("PHI"), lead[2023].get("IND")
top = {s: lead[s].index[0] for s in SEASONS}
non = m[~m["is_rpo"]]
epa_npass, epa_nrun = non.loc[non["play_type"] == "pass", "epa"].mean(), non.loc[non["play_type"] == "run", "epa"].mean()
sd_rpo, sd_non = rpo["epa"].std(), non["epa"].std()
gun_rpo = rpo["shotgun"].mean()
rank25 = {t: i + 1 for i, t in enumerate(lead[2025].index)}
```

Five things to read from @fig-rpo-data and the numbers behind it.

**RPOs are a small, steady slice of NFL offense.** FTN charted `{python} f"{rate[2022]:.1%}"` of plays as
RPOs in 2022, `{python} f"{rate[2023]:.1%}"` in 2023, `{python} f"{rate[2024]:.1%}"` in 2024 and
`{python} f"{rate[2025]:.1%}"` in 2025 (the 2024 dip is larger than PFF's and may partly be charting). The
leaders are the teams this chapter has already met: `{python} top[2022]` in 2022
(`{python} f"{phi22:.1%}"`), `{python} top[2023]` in 2023 (`{python} f"{ind23:.1%}"`), and Kansas City in
2025 (`{python} f"{kc25:.1%}"`), more than twice the league rate. At the other end, the RPO is plainly a
play-caller's choice, not a law of modern football. The 49ers and Rams, who run mostly from under center with
wide-zone blocking, are the bottom two in 2025 (`{python} f"{lead[2025]['SF']:.1%}"` and
`{python} f"{lead[2025]['LA']:.1%}"`): `{python} f"{gun_rpo:.0%}"` of the league's charted RPOs came from the
shotgun, and an offense that lives under center gets the same "make the linebacker step up, then throw behind
him" effect from play-action instead ([04-05](04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)). Yet the 2025 Packers, whose head
coach Matt LaFleur comes from the same Shanahan–McVay tree, ranked `{python} rank25['GB']`th. And Baltimore, with Lamar
Jackson, one of the league's most dangerous running quarterbacks, sits mid-table (`{python} f"{lead[2025]['BAL']:.1%}"`): a zone
read or a designed quarterback run is an option *run*, and FTN doesn't count it as an RPO.

**Most RPOs are runs.** On `{python} f"{gave_all:.0%}"` of the charted RPOs from 2022 to 2025 the ball was
handed off (`{python} f"{gave25:.0%}"` in 2025). That is the "run with a safety valve" idea from the Madden
callout, in data. It also means the RPO's main effect is invisible in a box score: its product is the
defender who wasn't in the run fit.

**NFL RPO throws are short, and very often behind the line.** `{python} f"{behind_r:.0%}"` of RPO throws were
caught (or aimed) at or behind the line of scrimmage, against `{python} f"{behind_o:.0%}"` of other passes;
only `{python} f"{deep_r:.0%}"` travelled more than ten yards in the air, against
`{python} f"{deep_o:.0%}"` of other passes. That shape is the clock at work: the bubbles and now screens come
out about half a second after the snap, before any lineman can drift a yard, and a throw beyond the line has
to leave so fast that it can't be far beyond it.

**The rule bites.** From 2022 to 2025 the NFL called `{python} str(idp_n)` ineligible-downfield fouls on
passes in the regular season. `{python} f"{idp_rpo:.0%}"` of them came on plays FTN charted as RPOs, though RPOs
were only `{python} f"{rpo_share:.1%}"` of plays: per snap, an RPO is many times more likely to draw the flag
than any other play.

**Per play, RPOs are about average, and steadier.** Split by branch, the numbers look dramatic: RPO throws
averaged `{python} f"{epa_pass:+.3f}"` EPA with a `{python} f"{comp_r:.0%}"` completion rate, against
`{python} f"{epa_npass:+.3f}"` for all other passes; RPO handoffs averaged `{python} f"{epa_run:+.3f}"`,
against `{python} f"{epa_nrun:+.3f}"` for all other runs. Don't read that as "the throws are great and the
runs are bad." It is *selection*, as with the quarterback keeps of 03-04: the quarterback throws precisely when
the throw is open and hands off when it isn't, so the throws are the good half of the reads by construction.
Put the halves back together and RPOs come out close to ordinary plays: `{python} f"{epa_rpo:+.3f}"` EPA per
play against `{python} f"{epa_non:+.3f}"`, and an EPA success rate of `{python} f"{sr_rpo:.1%}"` against
`{python} f"{sr_non:.1%}"`. What does differ is the spread. The standard deviation of EPA on RPOs is
`{python} f"{sd_rpo:.2f}"`, against `{python} f"{sd_non:.2f}"` on other plays: fewer disasters and fewer
explosions, which is what you'd expect from a play that throws only short and only when it's open.[^ftn]

The box count shows up, weakly, too: when FTN counted six defenders in the box,
`{python} f"{box_thrown[6]:.0%}"` of RPOs were thrown; with seven, `{python} f"{box_thrown[7]:.0%}"`; with
eight or more, `{python} f"{box_thrown[8]:.0%}"`. More defenders near the ball, more throws: the counting
logic of the bubble RPO, visible in charting that sees only the alignment at the snap.

PFF's charting, with its larger RPO count, tells a slightly different story: from 2021 to 2025, NFL RPOs gained
fewer yards per play than other plays (4.53 against 5.43) but were "successful" more often (52.3% against
48.1%).[^pffusage3] The two series don't contradict each other so much as measure different things. PFF uses its
own success definition, not the EPA-based one above, and its RPO count is about twice FTN's, so it includes
many snaps FTN called plain runs or passes. What both agree on is the shape: RPOs are **not big-play
machines**. They are a low-variance way to gain modest yardage with a run that is always blocked, and whether
they beat an ordinary play on efficiency depends on whose charting you trust.

## How defenses answer

Defenses have had a decade to study NFL RPOs, and the answers all attack one of the RPO's three parts: the
read, the throw, or the run behind it. This is a preview; the defense's side gets its full treatment in
[Run Fits: Gap Integrity, Force, Spill, and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd).

```{python}
#| label: fig-rpo-answer
#| fig-cap: "Making the read lie: one answer to the slant RPO of the earlier figure. The overhang safety (ringed) is told to play the slant no matter what, and he walls it at the snap, so the quarterback reads 'give.' But the free safety, deep in the middle, has a run job on this call, decided before the snap: he comes downhill the instant the ball is snapped, without waiting to read anything, into the backside of the box, the spot the overhang defender would have filled. The read was right and the run still meets an extra defender (the red X). The price: with the free safety in the box, nobody is left in the deep middle."
LAT, WIN = (-19.0, 6.5), (-7.0, 17.0)
dfn = only(nickel("single_high", LCB=(6.5, -16.4)), -20, 7)
p = Play(only(trips(), -20, 7), dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
for k, end in [("LT", (0.25, -4.2)), ("LG", (0.3, -2.2)), ("C", (0.35, 0.3)), ("RG", (0.35, 1.3)),
               ("RT", (0.3, 3.8)), ("Y", (0.35, 4.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
p.route("X", r.slant(stem=2.0, length=8.0))
go_to(p, "SS", (5.4, -11.0), "path")
go_to(p, "FS", (3.4, -1.4), "path", via=[(9.0, -1.0)])
go_to(p, "RB", (2.0, 0.4), "run", via=[(-4.6, -0.2), (-1.6, 1.4), (0.8, 0.9)])
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=LAT, window=WIN, width_in=5.9)
read_line(f, p, (-4.6, -0.5), (5.2, -8.6))
tackle_x(f, p, 2.6, -0.2)
say(f, p, 3.7, -14.7, "SS walls the slant:\nQ reads 'give'", color=RED, fontsize=6.8)
point_to(f, p, (11.4, 4.0), (8.0, -1.0), "FS comes down into\nthe box at the snap", fontsize=6.8, color=RED)
say(f, p, 15.2, -0.5, "deep middle: empty after the snap", fontsize=6.8, color=style.INK_2)
point_to(f, p, (9.0, -4.8), (2.6, -0.2), "the give meets\nthe safety", fontsize=6.6, shrink=5)
plt.show()
```

- **Read the line, not the back.** The most useful key a linebacker has against an RPO team is the
  [uncovered](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-covered-uncovered-lineman) guard, the one with no defensive
  lineman in front of him (03-01). If he climbs hard to the second level, it's a true run: he couldn't
  legally do that on a pass. If he stays at the line, sits, or blocks whoever is in front of him without
  climbing, it may be an RPO, and the linebacker plays his pass job first. The cost: the key is only as good
  as the offense's honesty, and offenses answer with true runs whose guards climb, to punish linebackers who
  wait.
- **Make the read lie.** Give the read defender a rule (always play the pass) and put someone else in his
  run fit, usually a safety *rotating down* after the snap (showing deep, then dropping toward the line), as
  in @fig-rpo-answer. It is the scrape exchange of 03-04 with a safety instead of a linebacker, and it's built
  on the post-snap rotations of
  [Disguise and Rotation](../06-pass-coverage/06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd#post-snap-rotation-part-1-two-high-becomes-one-high).
  It works because the safety's run job is *called*: he triggers at the snap without reading anything, so
  he arrives in time. The cost is the deep defender who left, and a play-action shot over him beats it.
- **Play two-high and fit the run from depth.** Two-high shells, especially the
  [quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarters) family of [06-05](../06-pass-coverage/06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)
  (a two-deep zone in which the safeties also help against the run), keep the overhang defender honest on the
  pass and let a safety who starts ten yards deep become the extra run defender once he sees a handoff.
  Against a pre-snap count, this is a defense that shows six in the box and plays like seven. Its weakness is
  the run itself. Unlike the rotating safety above, this one *reads first* (run or pass?) and only then comes
  down, so he arrives late, often after the back is already past the line.
- **Take away the conflict with man coverage.** In man coverage, the defender over the slot isn't torn
  between a gap and an area: he has a man, and he goes with him. Nobody is in conflict, so there's nothing to
  read. The price is the one man coverage always pays: defenders with their backs to the ball, and a box whose
  count the run can attack.
- **Squeeze the clock.** Hold the read defender's decision as long as possible (a bluff, a slow-play) so the
  quarterback rides the mesh a beat longer and the linemen, run blocking, drift past a yard. The flag is a
  defensive weapon too, and a defense that has watched the tape knows which linemen climb early. The cost: a
  defender who is still deciding is in neither job, so against an offense that just hands off on time, the
  run gets a defender who arrives a step late.
- **Hit the quarterback.** Every RPO exposes him for a moment with his eyes on one defender and his body
  turned toward the back. While he still holds the ball at the mesh he can be tackled like any ball carrier,
  and a rusher who arrives just as he throws may still finish the hit within a step of the release (later than
  that is roughing the passer).[^rtp] Pressure off the edge makes him hurry the read. The cost: the extra
  rusher comes from somewhere, usually the coverage, and the quick throws an RPO carries go to exactly the
  space he left.

Offenses answer back, as always: with motion that changes who the conflict defender is just before the snap,
with RPOs that read the *safety* instead of the overhang, and with play-action that looks exactly like the RPO
for the first second and then throws deep over the safety who has learned to come down. That conversation, how
one play makes the next one work, is the subject of
[Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd), where the RPO appears
as a [**constraint play**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-constraint-play): a play that punishes a defense
for overplaying the offense's base run.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: "Is he reading you?"** Every RPO has a defender being read. Find him before the snap and you'll see
the decision before the replay does.

*Before the snap*

- **Shotgun or pistol, back beside the quarterback, receivers spread.** That's the RPO look. Not every snap
  from it is an RPO, so treat it as "possible."
- **Count the box, then count outside.** Six or seven in the box? How many defenders are within seven yards of
  the line over the slot receivers? If the box is heavy and the slots are light, expect a throw (a bubble or
  now screen) the instant the ball is snapped.
- **Find the apex.** Who stands halfway between the box and a slot receiver? On the single-receiver side, is a
  safety walked down? That's the likely read. Say it out loud: "he's being read."

*At the snap*

- **RPO or play-action? Watch the line for half a second.** On an RPO the linemen fire *forward*, low, and
  stay on their blocks at the line; nobody climbs. On play-action they make one hard run step, then their
  helmets pop up and they settle into pass protection, often a step *behind* the line. And on a true run, the
  uncovered guard climbs to a linebacker. Forward and staying put means RPO.
- **Where the quarterback's head turns.** On a plain handoff, he looks at the back. On a zone read, his eyes
  are on a defensive *lineman* at the line. On a post-snap RPO they go to the *second level* or out over a
  slot: **his eyes are on a defender**. On the live sideline shot you can usually see his helmet turn; for his
  actual eyes and the defender he's watching, wait for the end-zone replay ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd#the-other-angles-replays-the-end-zone-and-the-skycam)).
- **The backside receiver.** On a pure run he jogs or blocks his cornerback. On an RPO he runs a full-speed
  slant or glance, because he might get the ball.
- **Watch the read defender's first two steps, not the ball.** Forward and inside: predict *throw*, behind
  him. Backward, widening, or eyes on a receiver: predict *give*.
- **Count to one.** If the ball isn't out of the quarterback's hand by about a second, it's probably a handoff.
  (Play-action's throw comes later, two and a half seconds or more, after a full fake and a drop.)

*After the play*

- **On the replay, freeze the frame when the ball leaves the quarterback's hand and look at the linemen.** Is
  anyone more than a yard past the line without a defender in his hands? That's the flag the umpire is looking
  for. Did one get thrown?
- **On the next snap,** did the read defender do the opposite? Defenses adjust within a drive.

For your prediction log ([01-06](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)): on every RPO look, write
the defender you think is being read and your call (G or T) from his first steps; afterward, write what happened.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1: count both sides.** First-and-10 at midfield. The offense is in the shotgun, 11 personnel, trips to
the right with the tight end attached, the back offset left. It has thrown the bubble RPO twice already today. This
time the defense shows the picture below before the snap. Count the box and count outside the box on the trips
side. Hand off or throw the bubble? And is there anything on the left side the quarterback should like?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: first-and-10, gun 11 personnel, trips right with the tight end attached. The defense has the nickel back over H and the strong safety walked down outside him, six yards deep; the free safety is alone in the deep middle."
p = Play(trips(), nickel("single_high", NB=(5.0, 9.6), SS=(6.0, 13.4), FS=(13.5, 0.0)), los=60, to_go=10)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.5, 20.0), window=(-7.2, 15.6), width_in=6.0)
panel_title(f.ax, "Drill 1: 1st and 10, the trips side crowded")
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Hand off, and the left side is the bonus.**

- **The box:** four linemen and two linebackers, six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the
  tight end). A hat on every hat: the run is fairly blocked.
- **Outside on the trips side:** H and Z against the nickel back, the cornerback and the strong safety, all
  within seven yards of the line. Two against three: the bubble is dead. The defense has done exactly what
  two thrown bubbles teach it to do.
- **The left side:** to get that third defender over the trips side *and* keep six in the box, the defense
  has left X alone against an off cornerback, with the only safety in the middle of the field. A slant or
  glance to X is the throw the count favors, if the play has one packaged to that side (many RPOs pair a
  bubble on one side with a slant or glance on the other, for exactly this picture).

The general lesson: the count is never just one side. A defense that wins the numbers in one place has lost
them somewhere else, and a pre-snap RPO is a machine for finding where.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2: freeze frame.** Second-and-8. The offense runs the slant RPO of @fig-slant-rpo to the left, the
inside-zone run going right. The picture below is frozen about six tenths of a second after the snap, with the
ball in the back's belly at the mesh. The overhang safety (ringed) has taken two quick steps, and his
shoulders have turned square to the backfield. Does the quarterback give or throw? What happens if the cornerback had lined up on X's inside shoulder instead?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the slant RPO, about 0.6 seconds after the snap. Players are drawn where they stood at the snap; the lines show where each has gone by the moment of the read: the line run-blocking right, the back arriving at the mesh, X two steps into his stem, and the overhang safety's first two steps."
dfn = only(nickel("single_high", LCB=(6.5, -16.4)), -20, 7)
p = Play(only(trips(), -20, 7), dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
for k, end in [("LT", (0.25, -4.2)), ("LG", (0.3, -2.2)), ("C", (0.35, 0.3)), ("RG", (0.35, 1.3)),
               ("RT", (0.3, 3.8)), ("Y", (0.35, 4.6))]:
    go_to(p, k, end)
go_to(p, "X", (1.4, -15.0), "route")
go_to(p, "SS", (3.6, -6.9), "path")
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.6, -0.3), "path")
p.highlight("SS", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-19.0, 6.8), window=(-7.0, 14.6), width_in=5.6)
panel_title(f.ax, "Drill 2: 2nd and 8, frozen at the mesh")
read_line(f, p, (-4.8, -0.4), (3.6, -6.9))
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Throw the slant.** In six tenths of a second the safety has come two yards forward and two yards inside:
shoulders toward the run, eyes in the backfield. He has chosen the run, and in doing so he has left the slant's
landing spot, five yards past the line where he was standing. The quarterback pulls the ball and throws it on
time, before the linemen have had a chance to drift past a yard. The cornerback, seven yards off and outside,
can't get there. (Compare @fig-slant-rpo: this is its upper branch.)

**If the cornerback had lined up inside**, the slant would have been a bad throw no matter what the safety
did: the corner sits on the route's path. The quarterback would know that before the snap, and on a well-built
call he'd have a second answer on that side (a quick out or a bubble) or he'd treat the play as a straight
handoff. Leverage picks the live route; the read picks whether to throw it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3: flag or no flag?** A glance RPO goes for 15 yards. On the replay, frozen at the instant the ball left
the quarterback's hand, you see the picture below. The left guard blocked the 3-technique at the line, let
go, and is now about two and a half yards past the line on his way to the Will. The right tackle engaged the
7-technique at the line and has driven him two yards backward, still locked on. Is there a foul in an NFL game?
In a college game?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: the instant of the throw. The left guard (ringed) is about two and a half yards past the line of scrimmage with no defender in his hands; the right tackle (ringed) is two yards past it, still blocking the defensive end he engaged at the line. The pass is on its way to X."
base = only(trips(), -18, 7)
spots = {"LT": (0.9, -4.3), "LG": (2.5, -2.9), "C": (0.3, -0.4), "RG": (0.3, 1.3), "RT": (1.8, 4.0),
         "Y": (0.0, 5.8), "QB": (-5.4, -1.2), "RB": (-3.6, 0.9), "X": (7.2, -13.2)}
dspots = {"BE": (1.9, -4.9), "BT": (1.4, -1.3), "PT": (1.9, 0.45), "PE": (2.9, 4.3),
          "WILL": (5.4, -3.8), "MIKE": (3.8, 1.8), "LCB": (11.0, -16.0), "FS": (12.6, -8.2)}
off = [q.moved(d=spots[q.key][0], w=spots[q.key][1]) if q.key in spots else q for q in base]
dfn = [q.moved(d=dspots[q.key][0], w=dspots[q.key][1]) if q.key in dspots else q
       for q in only(nickel("two_high"), -18, 7)]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("LG", "RT", color=style.SERIES[6])
f = draw(p, lateral=(-17.5, 8.5), window=(-6.4, 14.2), width_in=5.6)
region(f, p, 0.0, 1.0, -17.4, 8.4, style.MUTED, alpha=0.10, lw=0.6, ls=(0, (2, 2)))
throw(f, p, (-5.4, -1.2), (11.2, -11.6), rad=-0.1)
point_to(f, p, (7.8, -0.8), (2.5, -2.9), "LG: 2½ yards past,\nhands empty", fontsize=6.6)
point_to(f, p, (7.4, 5.0), (1.8, 4.0), "RT: 2 yards past,\nstill blocking", fontsize=6.6)
say(f, p, 1.5, -12.6, "1 yard", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2)
panel_title(f.ax, "Drill 3: the ball is out")
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**NFL: yes, on the left guard; the right tackle is fine.** Illegal man downfield, five yards from the previous
spot, and the 15-yard completion comes back. The guard engaged the 3-technique within a yard of the line, but he
*let go* and kept moving forward, which the rule forbids once he's past a yard. The right tackle is legal under
the rule's exception: he made contact at the line on his initial charge and has stayed locked on while driving his
man downfield.

**College: no foul.** The limit is three yards beyond the neutral zone, and the guard, about two and a half
yards past the line of scrimmage, is inside it. He hasn't reached the Will yet, which matters too: had he
already been blocking him that far downfield, college could call offensive pass interference instead. The right tackle is legal under either rulebook.

This is the NFL RPO's whole problem in one frame. The guard did exactly what inside zone teaches: a first block
and a climb to the backside linebacker. That's why NFL coaches either keep the guard on his first block when the
play might be a pass, or read the Will instead of climbing to him, which is the glance RPO.
:::

## Takeaways

- An **RPO** blocks a run and carries a pass on the same snap, and the quarterback picks one. Unlike
  **play-action**, the run is real; unlike the **option**, one branch is a pass. Every RPO is a **packaged play**.
- It attacks a **conflict defender** with a run job and a pass job, most often the **apex or overhang defender**,
  sometimes a linebacker or a safety. If he plays the run, throw behind him; if he plays the pass, hand off. The
  run is the default.
- **Pre-snap RPOs** (the **bubble RPO**) are decided by counting the box against the defenders outside;
  **post-snap RPOs** (the **glance**, slant and stick RPOs and the **pop pass**) are decided by watching one
  defender at the mesh. The read does a blocker's job.
- The NFL's **illegal man downfield** rule (one yard, for any forward pass, with an exception for linemen still
  engaged with a defender they met at the line) makes NFL RPOs quick and short and keeps NFL linemen near the
  line; college's three yards past the neutral zone, only for passes that cross it, lets college RPOs
  run-block longer and throw farther.
- RPOs grew out of Air Raid tags, the zone read and the college spread, and the Reid tree carried them to the NFL
  (the 2017 Chiefs and Eagles). In FTN's charting they are a few percent of NFL plays, mostly handoffs, with throws
  that cluster at or behind the line, and about as efficient per play as anything else, with less variance.
- Defenses answer by reading the line instead of the back (a guard who climbs means run), making the read lie
  (a safety called down into the vacated run fit), playing two-high and fitting from depth, playing man to
  remove the conflict, stretching the clock to draw flags, and hitting the quarterback. Each one gives
  something back: a deep defender, a step in the run fit, or a rusher's worth of coverage.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to tracking data.** The animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation written in NFL Big
Data Bowl coordinates (simulated, BDB-format), so real tracking data drops into the same drawing code. The 2025
Big Data Bowl's `plays.csv` carries a PFF run-pass-option flag (`pff_runPassOption`), so finding real RPOs is a
filter, not a hunt. With the tracking you can measure what this chapter only describes: how far past the line
each lineman is at the frame of the `pass_forward` event, and how long the quarterback held the mesh. The cell
below shows the shape of that code (it is not run, because the course does not download the Big Data Bowl files).

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real tracking data; not run)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
rpos = plays[plays["pff_runPassOption"] == 1]                    # PFF's RPO flag (BDB 2025)
g, pl = rpos.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.6, 1.0, 1.8])

# How far past the line is each offensive lineman when the ball is thrown?
los = one.loc[(one["frameType"] == "SNAP") & (one["side"] == "ball"), "x"].iloc[0]
throw_f = one.loc[one["event"] == "pass_forward", "frameId"].min()
linemen = one[(one["frameId"] == throw_f) & one["position"].isin(["T", "G", "C"])]
print((linemen["x"] - los).round(1).tolist())                  # yards past the line
```
:::

[^ftn]: This book's calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`load_pbp`) joined on game and play ID to FTN charting
    (`load_ftn_charting`, flag `is_rpo`), regular seasons 2022–2025, plays with `play_type` pass or run and a down
    (so scrambles and sacks on RPO looks are included; spikes and kneel-downs are not). Air yards: pbp `air_yards` on
    RPO passes. Box counts: FTN `n_defense_box`. Ineligible-downfield fouls: pbp `penalty_type == "Ineligible
    Downfield Pass"` on any regular-season play, joined to FTN's flag. EPA and success as defined in
    [Expected Points, EPA and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd).
